Saving the Working Families Tax Credit Expansions

What Hawaiʻi’s working families lose when the 2023 expansions of the state earned income tax credit, the food/excise tax credit and the child and dependent care tax credit expire after 2027, and what renewing them would cost.

Hawaiʻi Appleseed · Model run November 25, 2026 · Tax years 2028 to 2031

$83 million
in lost credits for working families in 2028 (give or take about $1 million), which is also what renewing them would cost the state.
189,000
households would receive less in credits in 2028.
$782
is the average loss for a single-parent household.

What Act 163 Did

IN 2023 THE LEGISLATURE DOUBLED Hawaiʻi’s two main tax credits for working families and expanded a third.1 Act 163 raised the state earned income tax credit from 20 percent to 40 percent of the federal credit, which already went only to people who work.2 It also more than doubled the refundable food/excise tax credit, which offsets the general excise tax low-income households pay on groceries and other necessities, and extended it $10,000 further up the income scale.3 And it raised the child care and other dependent care costs that count toward the refundable child and dependent care tax credit from $2,400 to $10,000 for one child or dependent, and from $4,800 to $20,000 for two or more. The credit itself, 15 to 25 percent of those costs depending on income, did not change.4

All three expansions were temporary. Act 163 is repealed on December 31, 2027, and all three credits return to their earlier form for tax year 2028. A 2026 bill to extend them was not enacted.5 The state earned income tax credit stays refundable, but at 20 percent of the federal credit.

The credit is a percentage of the work-related care spending up to these limits, and no more than the earnings of the lower-earning spouse. A family’s credit is 25 percent of the spending the credit counts at incomes up to $25,000, one point less for each further $5,000 and 15 percent above $50,000, so a household with $6,000 of care costs and an income of $20,000 receives $1,500 through 2027 and $600 after.

What Families Lose

WHEN THE EXPANSIONS EXPIRE, working families will receive about $83 million less in tax year 2028, with $40.3 million coming from the state earned income tax credit, $33.6 million from the food/excise tax credit and $9.2 million from the child and dependent care tax credit. Renewing all three would cost the state the same amount, about $335 million over tax years 2028 to 2031.6 Sampling error puts the 2028 loss within about $1 million either way (Table 8).

The food/excise credit’s amounts and income limits are not adjusted for inflation. As wages rise, fewer households qualify for the credit, and its value decreases. At its current level of expansion, the credit would provide $54 million in 2028 and $50 million in 2031. The state earned income tax credit follows the federal credit, which does increase with inflation.

Who Will Be Affected

THE LOSS FALLS HARDEST ON FAMILIES WITH CHILDREN and on the lowest incomes. Among the 20 percent of households with the lowest incomes, 76 percent would lose part of a credit in 2028, an average of $396 each, and that group would take 36 percent of the total loss. Single-parent households that lose part of a credit give up more, an average of $782 each, as Figure 2 shows.

Households are ranked by the combined income of everyone in them. Many Hawaiʻi households include several tax filers, so a grown child or grandparent with a low income can qualify on their own return in a household near the top of the ranking; that is why 30 percent of the top fifth lose some credit.

More Families in Poverty

LOSING THE EXPANSIONS DEEPENS POVERTY in 2028: families below the poverty line would fall a combined $20 million further short of it, and an estimated 4,200 more people would drop below the line, about 1,800 of them children. The state poverty rate rises from 10.7 percent to 11.0 percent, and for single parents and their children from 21.8 percent to 22.5 percent.

These figures use the Census Bureau’s Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts tax credits and public benefits as income and adjusts for Hawaiʻi’s cost of living. Because the counts come from a survey sample, they are rounded to the nearest hundred and carry a wide margin of error, with a 90 percent range of 3,200 to 5,200 people and 1,200 to 2,400 children (Table 8). The count is the average over 2,000 simulations of which families claim each credit and what each family spends on medical care, so it does not hinge on any one household near the line. The estimate is static and does not count parents who leave work when the credit shrinks, which the model’s separate analysis of the state earned income tax credit finds would add to the total.

How These Estimates Are Calculated

THE MODEL STARTS with Hawaiʻi households from the Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey, which records the age and relationship of each household member, and it grows their incomes forward using Congressional Budget Office projections. It places each child on a tax return with a parent when the survey shows who the parent is, including a grandchild who lives with a parent and grandparent, and it then calculates the federal earned income tax credit for each household, adjusted to match IRS counts of Hawaiʻi claimants, and uses the statute’s own schedules to calculate each state credit under both laws. For the child and dependent care tax credit, it uses what families with young children spend on child care in four years of the Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey, with the share of families who pay for care at each income level set from IRS records of the federal child care credit.

These estimates answer one question, which is how much less working families would receive if the expansions end. To answer it, the model calculates each credit twice for the same households, once under the expanded rules and once under the earlier rules that return in 2028, and the difference is the loss, which is the part of each credit that Act 163 added (Table 2a). The model assumes that the share of eligible families who claim each credit stays where it is today, and it leaves out any other change a household might face.

Because not every eligible household claims a credit, the model sets how many do by matching what the Department of Taxation actually paid, using the latest year the Department reports for each credit, which is 2024 for the state earned income tax credit (the new credit claimed that year)7 and 2023 for the food/excise and child and dependent care credits.8 The model then keeps that claim rate the same in every later year, and it holds the number of earned income tax credit claimants at the IRS count of Hawaiʻi returns, about the same in every year. History cannot yet say whether that is right: claims have been flat since 2022, but they fell 1 to 3 percent a year before the pandemic, and if that decline resumed, the later-year earned income tax credit figures here would be too high. As a test, the same rate applied to 2022, before the expansion, comes within 1 percent of what the Department paid for the food/excise credit that year under the old table, and within 1 percent of what it paid for the child and dependent care credit under the old limits (Table 5).

The Department of Taxation’s report on the state earned income tax credit also breaks down 2024 claims by income and by filing status, which makes it possible to check who the model says receives the credit, not only how much. For incomes under $55,000, the model’s dollars are within 19 percent of the Department’s in each of the four income ranges, while for incomes of $55,000 and above the model has $1.4 million against the Department’s $0.8 million. By filing status, the model gives heads of household 56.9 percent of the dollars against the Department’s 55.5 percent, gives married couples more (33.1 percent against 28.9 percent) and gives single filers less (10.0 percent against 15.3 percent). Because the statewide total is set to match the Department’s, these differences only shift losses between family types and do not change the statewide figure.

The Department’s filing-status table reports the credit applied, which includes older nonrefundable credits carried forward, so it is compared in shares. The model counts Hawaiʻi residents; they are 94.6 percent of the Department’s claims and 97.3 percent of its dollars.

These estimates can be off for two reasons. The first is that they start from a survey of fewer than 6,000 Hawaiʻi households, and a different group of households would have given somewhat different numbers. Table 8 shows how much difference to expect, using a method the Census Bureau provides for this purpose, and the true figure should fall inside each range about nine times in ten if the survey sample were the only source of error. The ranges for the credit dollars are narrow because the model is set to match what the Department of Taxation actually paid, so the survey only affects how that total grows to 2028 and how it splits between the expanded and the earlier credits. The ranges for poverty are wide because they count only a few thousand people near the poverty line, and a small survey sample captures few of them.

The second reason is that the model itself can be wrong, which a survey sample cannot measure. Table 5 checks it instead by comparing the model with the Department of Taxation’s records, and in years the model was not set to match, it came within 6 percent of the Department’s dollars for all three credits. Neither check covers the chance that incomes grow differently than the Congressional Budget Office projects, or that families respond to the change in ways the model does not capture.

Download the data

  • sampling_error_ty2028.csv: standard errors and 90 percent ranges for the loss and household figures (Table 8)
  • revenue_by_year.csv: all three credits by tax year, renewed and expired, with claimants
  • distribution_ty2028.csv: loss by fifth of households
  • by_family_type_ty2028.csv: loss by family type
  • by_credit_ty2028.csv: each credit’s loss, households that lose and average loss
  • poverty_ty2028.csv: poverty with the expansions renewed and expired
  • calibration.csv: claim rates and the checks in Table 5
  • eitc_check_ty2024.csv: the state earned income tax credit by income range and filing status, model and Department (Tables 6 and 7)
  • manifest.json: run parameters, inputs and code version
